title: Part 1, Chapter 49
paragraphs: Which treats of the shrewd conversation that Sancho Panza held with his master Don Quixote

"Aha, I've caught you," said Sancho. "This is what in my heart and soul I was longing to know. Come on now, señor, can you deny what people commonly say around here when somebody is out of sorts: 'I don't know what ails so-and-so, that he won't eat, or drink, or sleep, or give a proper answer to any question; you'd think he was enchanted'? From which it follows that those who don't eat, or drink, or sleep, or do any of the natural acts I'm talking about — those people are enchanted; but not those who have the desire your worship has, and drink when drink is given them, and eat when there's anything to eat, and answer every question put to them."

"What you say is true, Sancho," replied Don Quixote, "but I've already told you there are many kinds of enchantments; and it may be that in the course of time they've changed from one to another, and that now it may be the way with enchanted people to do all that I do, though they didn't do so before. So it's pointless to argue or draw inferences against the usage of the time. I know and feel that I am enchanted, and that is enough to ease my conscience; for it would weigh on me heavily if I thought I was not enchanted, and that in a faint-hearted and cowardly way I was letting myself lie in this cage, defrauding multitudes of the help I might give to those in need and distress, who at this very moment may be in dire want of my aid and protection."

"Still for all that," Sancho replied, "I say that, for your greater and fuller satisfaction, it would be well if your worship were to try to get out of this prison — and I promise to do all I can to help, and even to take you out of it — and see if you could once more mount your good Rocinante, who seems enchanted too, he's so melancholy and dejected. Then we might try our luck looking for adventures again; and if we have no luck there will be time enough to go back to the cage; in which, on the faith of a good and loyal squire, I promise to shut myself up alongside your worship, if you're so unfortunate, or I so stupid, as not to manage to carry out my plan."

"I'm content to do as you say, brother Sancho," said Don Quixote, "and when you see an opportunity for my release I'll obey you absolutely; but you'll see, Sancho, how mistaken you are in your view of my misfortune."

The knight-errant and the wayward squire kept up their conversation till they reached the place where the curate, the canon, and the barber, who had already dismounted, were waiting for them. The carter at once unyoked the oxen and left them to roam freely about the pleasant green spot, the freshness of which seemed to invite — not enchanted people like Don Quixote, but wide-awake, sensible folk like his squire, who begged the curate to allow his master to leave the cage for a little while; otherwise the prison might not be as clean as the dignity of a gentleman like his master required. The curate understood, and said he would happily comply, only that he feared his master, finding himself at liberty, would revert to his old ways and bolt off where no one could find him again.
"I'll answer for his not running away," said Sancho.
"And I as well," said the canon, "especially if he gives me his word as a knight not to leave us without our consent."

Don Quixote, who was listening to all this, said, "I give it; what's more, one who is enchanted as I am cannot do as he likes with himself; for the one who enchanted him could keep him from moving from one place for three ages, and if he tried to escape would bring him back flying." That being so, they might as well release him, particularly as it would be to everyone's advantage; for, if they didn't let him out, he warned that he wouldn't be able to avoid offending their nostrils unless they kept their distance.

The canon took his hand — even though they were still tied together — and on his word and promise they untied him, and he rejoiced beyond measure to find himself out of the cage. The first thing he did was stretch all over, then he went over to where Rocinante was standing, and giving him a couple of slaps on the haunches said, "I still trust in God and in his blessed mother, O flower and mirror of steeds, that we shall soon see ourselves, both of us, as we wish to be — you with your master on your back, and I mounted on you, following the calling for which God sent me into the world." Saying this, and accompanied by Sancho, he withdrew to a private spot, from which he came back much relieved and more eager than ever to put his squire's plan into action.

The canon studied him, marvelling at the extraordinary nature of his madness, and that in all his remarks and replies he showed such excellent sense, and only lost his stirrups, as has already been noted, when the subject of chivalry was broached. So, moved by compassion, he said to him, as they all sat on the green grass waiting for the provisions to arrive:

"Is it possible, my good sir, that the dull and idle reading of books of chivalry can have had such an effect on your worship as to upset your reason, so that you fancy yourself enchanted and the like — all as far from the truth as falsehood itself? How can any human understanding persuade itself that there ever was all that infinity of Amadises in the world, all that multitude of famous knights, all those emperors of Trebizond, all those Felixmartes of Hircania, all those palfreys and damsels-errant, and serpents, and monsters, and giants, and marvellous adventures, and enchantments of every kind, and battles, and prodigious encounters, splendid costumes, love-sick princesses, squires made counts, droll dwarfs, love letters, billing and cooing, swashbuckling women — in a word, all the nonsense the books of chivalry contain? For myself, I can only say that when I read them, as long as I don't stop to think they're all lies and trifles, they give me a certain amount of pleasure; but when I come to consider what they really are, I fling the very best of them at the wall, and would fling it into the fire if there were one at hand, as richly deserving such punishment — being cheats and impostors beyond the range of ordinary toleration, founders of new sects and modes of life, teachers who lead the ignorant public to believe and accept as truth all the folly they contain. And their audacity is such, they even dare to unsettle the wits of gentlemen of birth and intelligence, as is plainly shown by how they have served your worship, bringing you to such a pass that you have to be shut up in a cage and carried on an ox-cart like a lion or a tiger that's hauled around to make money by showing it off. Come, Señor Don Quixote, have some compassion for yourself, return to the bosom of common sense, and put to use the liberal share of it that heaven has been pleased to bestow upon you, employing your abundant gifts of mind in some other reading that may benefit your conscience and add to your honour. And if, still led away by your natural bent, you wish to read books of exploits and chivalry, read the Book of Judges in Holy Scripture, for there you'll find grand reality, and deeds as true as they are heroic. Lusitania had a Viriatus, Rome a Cæsar, Carthage a Hannibal, Greece an Alexander, Castile a Count Fernan Gonzalez, Valencia a Cid, Andalusia a Gonzalo Fernandez, Estremadura a Diego García de Paredes, Jerez a Garci Perez de Vargas, Toledo a Garcilaso, Seville a Don Manuel de Leon — to read of whose valiant deeds will entertain and instruct the loftiest minds and fill them with delight and wonder. Here, Señor Don Quixote, you'll find reading worthy of your sound understanding; from which you'll rise learned in history, in love with virtue, strengthened in goodness, improved in manners, brave without recklessness, prudent without cowardice — all to the honour of God, your own advantage, and the glory of La Mancha, where I am told your worship was born."
Don Quixote listened with the greatest attention to the canon's words, and when he found he had finished, after looking at him for some time, he replied:

"It appears to me, gentle sir, that your worship's argument is intended to persuade me that no knights-errant ever existed in the world, and that all the books of chivalry are false, lying, mischievous, and useless to the State, and that I have done wrong in reading them, worse in believing them, and worse still in imitating them when I undertook to follow the demanding calling of knight-errantry which they set out — for you deny that there were ever any Amadises of Gaul or of Greece, or any of the other knights of whom the books are full."

"It is exactly as you state it," said the canon. To which Don Quixote returned, "You also went on to say that books of this kind have done me a great deal of harm, in that they've upset my senses and got me shut up in a cage, and that it would be better for me to reform and change my reading, and read other, truer books which would afford more pleasure and instruction."
"Just so," said the canon.

"Well then," returned Don Quixote, "in my view it's you who are the one out of his wits and enchanted, since you have dared to utter such blasphemies against a thing so universally acknowledged and accepted as true that whoever denies it, as you do, deserves the same punishment you say you inflict on books that irritate you when you read them. For trying to persuade anyone that Amadis, and all the other knights-adventurers with whom the books are filled, never existed would be like trying to persuade him that the sun doesn't yield light, or ice cold, or earth nourishment. What wit in the world can persuade another that the story of Princess Floripes and Guy of Burgundy is not true, or that of Fierabras and the bridge of Mantible, which happened in the time of Charlemagne? By all that is good, it is as true as it is daylight now; and if it's a lie, then it must be a lie too that there was a Hector, or Achilles, or Trojan war, or Twelve Peers of France, or Arthur of England, who still lives changed into a raven and is endlessly looked for in his kingdom. One might just as well try to argue that the history of Guarino Mezquino, or the quest of the Holy Grail, is false; or that the loves of Tristram and Queen Yseult are made up, as well as those of Guinevere and Lancelot — when there are people who can almost remember having seen Dame Quintañona, who was the best cupbearer in Great Britain. And so true is this, that I recall a grandmother of mine on my father's side, whenever she saw any dame in a venerable hood, used to say to me, 'Grandson, that one looks like Dame Quintañona,' from which I conclude she must have known her, or at least seen some portrait of her. Then who can deny that the story of Pierres and the fair Magalona is true, when even to this day in the king's armoury you can see the pin with which the valiant Pierres steered the wooden horse he rode through the air, and it's a trifle bigger than the pole of a cart? Alongside the pin is Babieca's saddle, and at Roncesvalles there's Roland's horn, as large as a great beam; from which we may infer that there were Twelve Peers, and a Pierres, and a Cid, and other knights like them — of the kind people commonly call adventurers. Or perhaps I'll be told too that there was no such knight-errant as the valiant Lusitanian Juan de Merlo, who went to Burgundy and in the city of Arras fought with the famous lord of Charny, Mosen Pierres by name, and afterwards in the city of Basle with Mosen Enrique de Remesten, coming out of both encounters covered with fame and honour; or the adventures and challenges achieved and delivered, also in Burgundy, by the valiant Spaniards Pedro Barba and Gutierre Quixada (from whose family I come in the direct male line), when they vanquished the sons of the Count of San Polo. I shall be told too that Don Fernando de Guevara did not go in search of adventures to Germany, where he engaged in combat with Micer George, a knight of the house of the Duke of Austria. I shall be told that the jousts of Suero de Quiñones, him of the 'Paso,' and the enterprise of Mosen Luis de Falces against the Castilian knight Don Gonzalo de Guzman, were mere mockeries; as well as many other achievements of Christian knights of these and foreign realms, which are so authentic and true that, I repeat, anyone who denies them must be totally wanting in reason and good sense."
The canon was astonished to hear the medley of truth and fiction Don Quixote was producing, and to see how well acquainted he was with everything relating to his knight-errantry; so he said in reply:

"I cannot deny, Señor Don Quixote, that there is some truth in what you say, especially as regards the Spanish knights-errant. I'm willing to grant too that the Twelve Peers of France existed, but I'm not prepared to believe that they did all the things Archbishop Turpin relates of them. The truth of the matter is they were knights chosen by the kings of France, called 'Peers' because they were all equal in worth, rank, and prowess (or at least if they weren't they ought to have been); and it was a kind of religious order like those of Santiago and Calatrava today, in which it is taken for granted that those who take it on are valiant knights of distinction and good birth. Just as we say now 'a Knight of St. John,' or 'of Alcántara,' they used to say then 'a Knight of the Twelve Peers,' because twelve equals were chosen for that military order. That there was a Cid, as well as a Bernardo del Carpio, there can be no doubt; but that they did the deeds people say they did, I hold to be very doubtful. As for the other matter — the pin of Count Pierres you mention, and say is near Babieca's saddle in the Armoury — I confess my sin: I am either so stupid or so short-sighted that, though I've seen the saddle, I've never been able to spot the pin, despite its being as big as your worship says."
"For all that, it is there, no doubt about it," said Don Quixote; "and what's more, they say it is enclosed in a sheath of cowhide to keep it from rusting."

"All that may be," replied the canon; "but by the orders I have taken, I don't recall seeing it. However, granting that it's there, that's no reason why I'm obliged to believe the stories of all those Amadises and of the whole multitude of knights they tell us about; nor is it reasonable that a man like your worship, so worthy, with so many good qualities and endowed with such a sound understanding, should let himself be persuaded that the wild crazy things written in those absurd books of chivalry are really true."
